paper_metadata.title: Pricing multi-asset derivatives by variational quantum algorithms

summary: The paper proposes a variational quantum algorithm for derivative pricing by solving the discretized Black–Scholes PDE with variational quantum simulation and estimating the option value via a SWAP‑test overlap. Numerical simulations on a statevector simulator use 4–6 qubits and hardware‑efficient ansätze (up to 30 parameters) to price a single‑asset double‑barrier option, showing qualitative agreement with classical finite‑difference solutions and the analytical formula. The authors analytically argue that their method avoids the classical O((1/ε)^{O(d)}) scaling of finite‑difference methods, but no empirical quantum advantage is demonstrated.

experiments.description: Variational quantum simulation of the discretized Black-Scholes PDE for pricing a single-asset double barrier option, with the derivative price recovered from the inner product between the evolved price state and the asset-price probability distribution state.

algorithm.variant: variational quantum simulation (VQS) for linear ODE/PDE evolution with SWAP-test overlap estimation
algorithm.ansatz: hardware-efficient ansatz with layers of RY gates and CZ entangling layers
algorithm.optimizer: McLachlan variational principle with classical Euler integration of the parameter ODE
algorithm.parameter_initialization: VQS starts from parameters set so the ansatz is identity at τ=0; for the separate initial-state fitting demo, L-BFGS-B is used to optimize parameters

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Uniform grid discretization of the asset-price domain; one computational basis state per grid point, with ngr=2^n grid points for n qubits
problem_formulation.objective_function: Solve the discretized Black-Scholes PDE backward in time and compute V(0,s0) via e^{-rt_ter}⟨p(t_ter)|V(t_ter)⟩
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Boundary conditions encoded through the inhomogeneous term C(τ) in the ODE; double knock-out barrier conditions in the experiment

dataset_specification.benchmark_name: analytical Black-Scholes barrier-option solution used as reference
dataset_specification.preprocessing: Finite-difference discretization of the Black-Scholes PDE; probability distribution from analytical geometric Brownian motion

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: No market dataset; parameters fixed to a synthetic Black-Scholes setup. The paper compares VQS results against the analytical solution and classical FDM with 16, 32, and 64 grid points.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Numerical simulation on a statevector-style simulator; comparison of estimated prices against the analytical solution across time and across qubit/layer settings

hardware.classical_solver: Euler method for ODE parameter updates; L-BFGS-B for initial-state fitting demo

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Analytical probability distribution of geometric Brownian motion; classical finite-difference discretization of the PDE; analytical barrier-option formula used for validation
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Inner product between simulated states; discounting by e^{-rt_ter} to obtain present price

speedup_claims.factor: O(poly(d log(1/epsilon))) for VQS/state preparation; SWAP-test measurements O(1/epsilon^2 (log(1/epsilon))^d)
speedup_claims.conditions: under the paper's assumptions for state preparation and bounded overlap factor; gate-based quantum computing only
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states the overall complexity is heuristic for the variational part; the SWAP-test measurement count still has exponential dependence in d through (log(1/epsilon))^d, but avoids factors like (1/epsilon)^{O(d)}.

speedup_claims.conditions: for the proposed overlap-based pricing method with sufficiently efficient state preparation and VQS
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a claimed asymptotic advantage, not an end-to-end hardware demonstration.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(poly(d log(1/ϵ))) for the VQS and state-preparation parts; SWAP-test measurements scale as O(1/ϵ^2 (log(1/ϵ))^d) under the paper's assumptions
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Classical finite-difference method scales as O((1/ϵ)^{O(d)})

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: not provided; theoretical analysis suggests polynomial improvement in ε but still exponential dependence on dimension through measurement scaling
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Requires efficient state preparation of probability distributions and payoff states, many SWAP‑test measurements O(1/ε² (log(1/ε))^d), and larger logical quantum circuits implementing VQS for high‑dimensional BSPDE grids
limiting_factors: variational solver heuristic with unknown convergence scaling
state preparation assumed efficient but not demonstrated
measurement cost grows exponentially with number of assets
classical PDE solvers already efficient for low‑dimensional problems

notes: Hardware inferred as simulator_statevector because the paper states numerical simulations using NumPy and does not name a physical QPU.
Num_qubits reported from the numerical experiments (4, 5, 6 qubits); the first listed case is used here as the representative resource entry.
Circuit depth not explicitly reported as a single number; the paper reports ansatz layers (2 and 4) and a depth-m circuit figure, but no total compiled depth.
The experiment includes a separate classical L-BFGS-B initial-state fitting demonstration, but the main quantum experiment is VQS + SWAP test.
The paper's claimed asymptotic improvement is polynomial in precision/dimension relative to classical FDM, not a proven end-to-end speedup.
Authors claim asymptotic improvement by removing factors like (1/ε)^{O(d)} compared to classical FDM.
However the paper demonstrates only small noiseless simulations (≤6 qubits) on a single‑asset example.
No empirical runtime comparison showing quantum outperforming classical methods.

experiments.description: Variational state‑preparation experiment demonstrating that a hardware‑efficient ansatz can approximate the payoff function state used as the BSPDE terminal condition.

algorithm.variant: variational state preparation via fidelity maximization
algorithm.ansatz: RY + CZ hardware-efficient ansatz (6 qubits, 6 layers)
